title: A World Powered by Muscle, Wind and Water
summary: Long ago there were no engines at all. People, horses, rushing rivers and windy hills did every bit of work. But deep under the ground, mines were filling up with water, and nobody could pump it out fast enough.

sections.heading: A World Without Engines
paragraphs: Close your eyes and imagine a world with no engines of any kind. No cars, no trains, no electric motors humming inside fridges, no power station somewhere far away sending electricity down a wire. If you wanted something to move, something alive or something natural had to move it. That was the world almost everyone lived in for thousands of years, right up until about 300 years ago.

In that world, the word 'power' meant muscles first of all. Farmers dug fields with spades and hoes. Women and children ground grain into flour by rubbing it between heavy stones, a job that could take hours every single day. Builders carried stone on their backs, sawyers cut planks by pulling a long saw up and down a pit, and sailors hauled ropes until their hands were raw. Rowers pushed great warships across the Mediterranean Sea with oars.

How much power is in a human body? Scientists today measure power in watts, the same unit printed on a light bulb. A healthy adult can keep working steadily all day at only about 70 to 75 watts. That is roughly enough to keep one old-fashioned light bulb glowing. For a short burst, such as sprinting up a staircase, a person might manage close to 900 watts, but nobody can keep that up for more than a few seconds. Muscles get tired, and tired people need food, water, sleep and rest.

Because one person is so weak, big jobs needed many people, and clever tools to multiply their strength. Levers, ramps, pulleys and wheels let a team move things far heavier than any one of them could lift alone. Roman engineers built cranes with a system of pulleys called a polyspastos. Worked by four men at a winch, one of these cranes could lift about 3,000 kilograms, about the weight of two small cars.

Even better was the treadwheel. Picture a giant wooden hamster wheel, taller than a house, with people walking inside it. As they walked, the wheel turned, winding a rope around its axle and lifting a heavy stone into the air. Because the wheel was so big compared with the axle, a couple of walkers could raise loads that would have needed a whole crowd pulling on ropes. In the Middle Ages, treadwheel cranes came back into use to build Europe's great cathedrals. They were set up inside the half-built walls and moved higher as the building grew.

You can still see real ones today. A treadwheel crane in the English harbour town of Harwich was built in 1667 and has two wheels side by side. Another, at Guildford in Surrey, dates from around 1700. They look like strange, enormous toys, but for centuries they were some of the most powerful lifting machines in the world, and every bit of their power came from people walking.

sections.heading: Horses in Circles: Gins and Whims
paragraphs: Animals were the next step up. Oxen pulled ploughs and heavy carts in slow, steady lines. Donkeys and mules carried loads along mountain paths. Horses were faster and stronger, and over the centuries farmers and miners found clever ways to borrow their strength for jobs that had nothing to do with pulling a cart.

The trick was to make the horse walk in a circle. Imagine a tall wooden post standing upright in the middle of a round, flat track. A long wooden arm sticks out sideways from the post, and a horse is harnessed to the end of the arm. As the horse plods round and round the track, the post turns with it. Gears or a big drum on the post can then turn that slow circular motion into almost anything: grinding grain, crushing apples for cider, threshing wheat, or winding a rope.

This machine was called a horse engine, a horse mill, or, in Britain, a horse gin. The word gin is short for engine, which once simply meant any clever device. Many farms in northern England and Scotland built round or many-sided sheds, called gin-gangs, to keep the horses and machinery out of the rain. A lot of these little buildings still stand next to old farmhouses today.

At mines, the horse gin had a special name: the whim. A whim had a wide wooden drum on top of its upright post. A rope wrapped around the drum ran out over pulleys and down the mine shaft. As the horse walked one way, the drum let one bucket down into the darkness while winding a full bucket up to the surface. Then the horse turned around and walked the other way. Whims hauled coal, rock and ore, and they could also be hooked up to pumps to lift water. Horse whims were used at some coal mines until the end of the 1800s. A wooden gin wheel from 1844, which once worked at Langton and Pinxton collieries (coal mines) in the East Midlands, is kept today at the Nottingham Industrial Museum.

In 1556 a German doctor and mining expert named Georg Bauer, who wrote under the Latin name Georgius Agricola, published a famous book called De re metallica, which means 'On the Nature of Metals'. It was packed with 292 woodcut pictures showing how miners worked. Some of them show horses walking in circles beside a mine, turning machines that pulled up water. Agricola explained that one of his pumps could only lift water about 24 feet (about 7 metres), so deep mines needed whole chains of pumps, one above the other. His book stayed the standard guide to mining for about 180 years.

Horses were strong, but they were not magic. Scientists who measured horses at a fair in Iowa in 1925 found that a big horse could produce nearly 15 horsepower for a few seconds. Over a whole working day, though, a horse can only keep up about one horsepower, a small fraction of its short-burst strength. And every horse needed hay and oats, water, a stable, a blacksmith for its shoes, and people to look after it. A busy mine might need dozens of horses working in shifts, eating their way through fields of crops. Keeping all those animals was expensive, and the deeper a mine went, the more of them it needed.

sections.heading: The Mighty Waterwheel
paragraphs: If you have ever held your hand in a fast stream, you have felt how hard moving water pushes. People realized long ago that a river never gets tired. It flows day and night, summer and winter, and it never needs feeding. All you have to do is put a wheel in its way.

Greek engineers were building waterwheels and toothed gears in the 3rd century BCE, more than 2,200 years ago. Greek and Roman writers described water-powered mills for grinding grain. The Roman architect Vitruvius gave the first known technical description of a watermill in the 1st century BCE. By about 70 CE, the Roman writer Pliny the Elder mentioned water-powered hammers working across much of Italy.

The most impressive ancient example was at Barbegal, near the town of Arles in southern France. In the 2nd century CE, the Romans built a hillside there with 16 waterwheels arranged in two long rows, like a staircase of wheels. Water from an aqueduct poured from one wheel down to the next. Experts estimate the mills could grind about 4.5 tonnes of flour a day, perhaps enough bread for around 12,500 people. Historians have called it the greatest known concentration of mechanical power in the ancient world.

Waterwheels came in different shapes. An undershot wheel dips its paddles into a flowing stream and is pushed along by the current. An overshot wheel has water poured onto it from above, into little buckets around its rim, so the weight of the falling water turns it. Overshot wheels are usually more efficient, but they need a waterfall or a channel bringing water down from higher ground. Breastshot wheels take the water about halfway up.

How does a turning wheel grind flour? With gears. In a typical mill, the waterwheel turns slowly on a thick wooden axle. A big wooden gear wheel on that axle, with pegs sticking out like teeth, meshes with a much smaller gear. Because the small gear has fewer teeth, it has to spin several times for every single turn of the big one. That smaller gear turns an upright shaft, and on top of that shaft sits the runner stone, a heavy round millstone spinning just above a fixed bed stone. Grain trickles into a hole in the middle of the runner stone and comes out at the edges as flour. Some clever mills, called tide mills, were built on the coast. They trapped seawater in a pond at high tide and let it flow out through the wheel as the tide went down.

In Europe in the Middle Ages, watermills spread almost everywhere. In 1085, William the Conqueror, the Norman king who had taken over England, sent officials to every county to record who owned what. The result, finished around 1086, was the Domesday Book. It lists 5,624 mills, and because the record is incomplete, the real number was probably higher. By about 1300, England may have had 10,000 to 15,000 mills. They ground grain, but water power was also used for sawing wood, pounding cloth to thicken it (called fulling), making paper and hammering iron.

But waterwheels had a big weakness: they could not move. A mill had to be built exactly where the right river was, and the work had to come to it. In a dry summer, the stream might shrink to a trickle and the wheel would stop. In a hard winter it could freeze solid. After heavy rain, floods could smash the wheel to pieces. And many of the places where power was needed most, such as the tops of hills where miners were digging, had no fast river nearby at all.

sections.heading: Catching the Wind
paragraphs: Wind was the other great natural power. Sailors had used it for thousands of years to push ships across seas and oceans. Turning wind into power on land took longer.

Hero of Alexandria, a Greek engineer you will meet properly in the next part, described a little wind-wheel that worked an organ in the 1st century CE, but it was more of a clever demonstration than a working mill. The first windmills that we know were really used for work appeared in Persia (modern Iran) and the neighbouring region of Khorasan, roughly between 700 and 900 CE. These early mills had sails that spun around an upright post, a bit like a revolving door, and they were used to grind grain and pump water.

In north-west Europe, windmills with sails turning on a horizontal shaft (the kind you probably picture) appeared in the 1100s. One of the earliest certain records is from 1185, at Weedley in Yorkshire, England. The first common type was the post mill. The whole wooden body of the mill, with its sails and millstones, sat balanced on one massive upright post, and the miller pushed a long tail pole to swing the entire building round so the sails faced into the wind. Later came tower mills, where only the cap on top of a stone or brick tower turned, and smock mills with wooden sides.

The Dutch became famous masters of wind power. Much of the Netherlands is low, flat land, some of it below sea level, and windmills were used from the 1400s onwards to pump water out of marshes and lakes and into drainage channels. Bit by bit, wind-powered pumps helped turn soggy wetland into farmland. Around 1850 the Netherlands had about 10,000 windmills, and roughly 1,000 still stand today. Across Europe, by about 1850 there may have been around 200,000 windmills and roughly 500,000 waterwheels working.

Wind power had its own problems, though. The wind does not blow when you want it to. On a calm day, the sails hang still. In a storm, a miller had to stop the sails before they spun so fast that the machinery caught fire from friction or the sails tore off. Windmills had to be built on open, exposed ground, and like waterwheels, they could not be picked up and moved to wherever a new job was waiting. Nobody could promise a mine owner that the wind would keep his pumps running through a still, foggy week.

sections.heading: Running Short of Wood, Turning to Coal
paragraphs: For heat, people mostly burned wood. Wood, and charcoal made by slowly baking wood, cooked food, warmed homes, fired pottery and bricks, boiled salt out of seawater, brewed beer and smelted iron. Forests also supplied timber for houses and, very importantly, for building ships.

In Britain, by the middle of the 1500s, wood was getting scarcer and more expensive, especially near growing towns like London. The population was rising, and forests had been cut down for farmland and fuel over many centuries. Historians still argue about how serious this 'wood crisis' really was. Some think it was a true national shortage, while others think it was mostly a local problem of prices in big towns, made worse by the cost of carrying heavy wood long distances. But everyone agrees on what happened next: more and more people switched to burning coal.

Coal was not new. The Romans had dug coal in Britain and burned it to heat bath houses and forts along Hadrian's Wall. But many people disliked it. It was smoky, smelly and dirty, and its critics mocked it with rude names, including 'the devil's excrement'. Still, coal had one huge advantage: a lump of coal holds much more heat energy than a lump of wood of the same weight, and Britain was sitting on enormous amounts of it.

So the coal trade boomed. Ships carried coal from Newcastle down the east coast to London in such numbers that the phrase 'carrying coals to Newcastle' later came to mean doing something pointless. In 1575 a Scottish businessman, George Bruce of Carnock, opened a remarkable mine at Culross on the Firth of Forth. He even built an artificial island out in the water and sank a shaft from it, with extra shafts for drainage and fresh air. By 1700 Britain was producing just under 3 million tons of coal a year, far more than any other country.

Coal did not only warm homes. It boiled seawater in huge iron pans to make salt along the coasts of Scotland and north-east England. It heated kilns for burning limestone into lime, which farmers spread on fields and builders used in mortar. Brewers, dyers, soap makers, glassmakers and brick makers all learned to use it in place of wood. Smelting iron with coal was much harder, because impurities in the coal spoiled the metal, and that problem would not be properly solved until the 1700s. Still, more and more of Britain's daily life was running on the black rock dug out from under its fields.

There was a catch. The easy coal, lying near the surface, was dug out first. To keep up with demand, miners had to follow the seams deeper and deeper underground. Before 1800, pits around the River Tyne in north-east England already reached about 300 to 1,000 feet (about 90 to 300 metres) down. It was not only coal, either. In Cornwall, in the far south-west of England, miners were chasing veins of tin and copper deep into the rock, and in Derbyshire and the north of England they dug for lead.

sections.heading: Mines That Kept Filling With Water
paragraphs: Dig a hole on a beach, and after a little while its bottom fills with water. The same thing happens underground, on a much bigger scale. Rainwater soaks down through soil and cracks in the rock, and much of the ground below us is full of this hidden groundwater. When miners dig a shaft and tunnels, water trickles, seeps and sometimes gushes in from the walls. The deeper the mine, the more water tends to pour in, and every bucket of it has to be lifted all the way back to the surface.

If the water is not removed, the mine floods. Tools, tunnels and valuable coal or ore disappear under a black, icy lake. Sometimes miners broke into old flooded workings by accident and the water rushed in suddenly, which was extremely dangerous. For mine owners, water was the enemy that could end a mine forever.

Miners fought back in several ways. The cheapest was to let gravity do the work. Where a mine was on a hillside, they dug a long, gently sloping drainage tunnel called an adit from the low ground into the hill, so water could run out by itself. In the lead mines of Derbyshire these tunnels were called soughs (said 'suffs'). In Cornwall, a huge network called the Great County Adit was dug during the 1700s and early 1800s, eventually stretching about 40 miles (about 64 kilometres) and draining more than 100 mines. But an adit can only drain a mine down to its own level. Anything dug deeper than the adit still floods.

Below that level, the water had to be lifted. Miners used buckets on ropes wound up by whims, chains of buckets on a loop, and pumps worked by people, horses or waterwheels. In the 1600s many British collieries used chain pumps driven by waterwheels. But each of these methods had a ceiling. Horses were expensive and slow. Waterwheels needed a good river nearby. And pumps had a strange limit that puzzled everyone.

Most simple pumps of the time were suction pumps, which work a bit like sucking a drink up a straw. However strong the pump and however hard you worked it, a suction pump could not raise water more than about 10 metres (about 33 feet) in one go. A measurement made in Italy around 1635 put the limit at about 18 Florentine yards, which is about the same. The great scientist Galileo was asked to explain it and got it wrong. The real answer, which involves the weight of the air itself, is so important to the steam engine story that it gets a whole part of its own later on. For now, the key point is this: to drain a deep mine with suction pumps, you needed a whole staircase of pumps, one above the other, each lifting water to the next. That meant lots of machinery, lots of horses and lots of money.

As mines went deeper in the 1600s, some simply had to be abandoned with plenty of coal or metal still left in them, because the water won. The miners knew exactly where the treasure was. They just could not keep it dry.

sections.heading: The Big Question: Could Fire Do the Work?
paragraphs: Look at the situation from a mine owner's point of view around the year 1690. You are sitting on a fortune in coal or tin. Your problem is water. Muscles, human or horse, are weak, tired and hungry. Rivers and wind are strong but stuck in one place and unreliable. You need a source of power that is strong, works day and night in any weather, and can be built right next to your mine shaft, wherever it is.

Now notice something odd. At a coal mine, the one thing you have plenty of is fuel. Fire was everywhere in this world. Blacksmiths' forges, brick kilns, glass furnaces, bakers' ovens and kitchen hearths burned all day long. Everyone knew fire made heat. Everyone had seen a pot of water boil, and seen the lid jiggle and rattle as steam escaped. But that heat simply drifted away up the chimney. Nobody had a machine that could turn the heat of a fire into steady, useful pushing and pulling.

That is the big question at the heart of this whole story: could heat be turned into motion? Could the burning of coal, instead of the eating of oats, lift water out of a mine, turn a millstone, or one day pull a cart? It sounds simple, but answering it would take the work of dozens of people in many countries over centuries. They would need to understand air, water, steam and a mysterious thing called a vacuum. They would need better metalworking, more accurate tools and a lot of courage, because steam can be dangerous.

When the answer finally came, it changed nearly everything about how people live and work, from the clothes we wear to the cities we live in and the electricity in our homes. But the idea did not appear out of nowhere in the 1700s. In fact, the idea that steam could make something move was already very old. Nearly two thousand years earlier, in a busy harbour city in ancient Egypt, an inventor had already made a ball spin with nothing but the steam from boiling water.

deepDive: How much power did the pre-industrial world really have? Historians and engineers have tried to put numbers on it. A person working steadily all day delivers only about 75 watts of useful mechanical power. A draught horse can sustain roughly ten times that, about one horsepower (around 750 watts), although it can briefly produce far more: measurements at the 1925 Iowa State Fair recorded a peak near 15 horsepower. Animals, however, come with hidden costs. A horse eats the produce of several acres of land a year, and for every hour of pulling it needs many hours of rest and care. Water and wind were the heavyweights. A large medieval watermill might deliver a few horsepower, and by about 1850 Europe may have had roughly half a million waterwheels and 200,000 windmills. The best ancient site, Barbegal in Roman Gaul, combined 16 wheels. Yet all of these sources shared a basic limitation that economists call being 'site-bound': the power was available only where the river ran or the wind blew, and only when nature cooperated. Mines exposed this limitation most painfully. Water flowing into a shaft must be lifted against gravity, and the work needed grows with both the amount of water and the depth. Doubling the depth doubles the work for each litre lifted, while deeper mines usually also let in more water. Suction pumps added a hard physical ceiling of about 10 metres per stage, because atmospheric pressure can support a water column only about that high. Historians debate the 'timber crisis' that is often said to have pushed Britain towards coal. Older accounts described a nationwide shortage; more recent research suggests that wood remained available in many regions and that high prices were concentrated in growing towns where transport costs were heavy. Either way, Britain's coal output rose to just under 3 million tons a year by 1700, and the problem of draining ever-deeper mines became a pressing economic issue. That is why the first commercial steam engines were not built to drive factories or vehicles, but to pump water.
funFact: When scientists measured working horses at the 1925 Iowa State Fair, one horse produced a burst of nearly 15 horsepower, even though over a whole day a horse can keep up only about one.

check.q: About how high can a simple suction pump lift water in one go?
wrong: There is no limit if you pump hard enough
